title: Object Lifetime, Dangling References and Safe Memory
learningObjectives: Explain object lifetime and dangling pointers/references.
Identify invalidation caused by destruction or vector reallocation.
Distinguish owning objects from non-owning views.
Use safe value returns and ownership types.

understand.concept: A dangling pointer/reference refers to an object whose lifetime has ended. Accessing it is undefined. Ownership and lifetime are the key safety questions.
understand.whyItMatters: Lifetime bugs cause subtle failures and security issues.
understand.explain: Avoid returning references to locals, invalidated vector elements, and pointers after deletion; use value returns or owning types.

examples.title: Do not return local address
examples.explanation: The local lifetime ends at return; this function is unsafe.

examples.title: Safe value return
examples.explanation: Returning a value copies or moves the result safely.

examples.title: Vector growth caveat
examples.code: std::vector<int> v{1,2};int* p=&v[0];v.push_back(3);\n// p may be invalidated if reallocation occurs
examples.explanation: Vector growth can invalidate pointers and references to its elements.

examples.title: Check owner lifetime
examples.explanation: view is non-owning and valid only while p keeps the object alive.

examples.title: Avoid use-after-delete
examples.code: auto p=std::make_unique<int>(6);\n// after p.reset(), its former pointee no longer exists
examples.explanation: Do not keep or dereference stale pointers after owner resets.

practise.guidedTask: For Object Lifetime, Dangling References and Safe Memory, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for Object Lifetime, Dangling References and Safe Memory. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.

Local lifetime ends after function returns.
The owner must keep the object alive.
reset releases ownership and destroys the object if solely owned.
